topic.title: Rusting, its prevention and the extraction of iron
topic.subject: science
topic.examWeightHint: Rusting shares one C2 question with redox most years, about 9 marks: the name of rust [2], the tubes experiment as one-mark identifications and purposes, and galvanising [2]. The blast furnace has carried a whole question of its own (Summer 2023 C2 Higher Q7, 11 marks, including two symbol equations and the slag).
mustMemorise: Rust is hydrated iron(III) oxide; rusting needs iron, water and oxygen
Anhydrous calcium chloride removes water; boiled water plus an oil layer removes oxygen
Barrier methods: painting, oiling or greasing, plastic coating, galvanising (a zinc coating)
Sacrificial protection: a more reactive metal, zinc or magnesium, corrodes in place of the iron
Blast furnace charge: haematite, coke and limestone, with hot air at the base
C + O2 → CO2; CO2 + C → 2CO; Fe2O3 + 3CO → 2Fe + 3CO2; CaO + SiO2 → CaSiO3
Slag floats on the molten iron, so it is tapped off higher up
Iron is used in bridges and structures because of its strength

sheet.howExamined: C2, 1 hour 15 minutes: 70 marks at Foundation, 80 at Higher, calculator and Chemistry Data Leaflet allowed. Rusting shares a question with redox. The name of rust is [2], marked as two separate points. Purposes of apparatus are [1] each with tight accept lists — the oil answer needs the word dissolving, and the drying-agent answer needs removes rather than keeps out. Galvanising is [2]: coated in zinc, then the reason. Furnace equations are marked reactants [1], product [1], balancing [1].

steps.decision: Two words, two marks: hydrated, and iron(III) oxide. Leaving out hydrated, or writing iron oxide without the (III), each costs one.

options: Because 'hydrated' and the oxidation state are separate marking points
Because iron only forms one oxide
Because rust contains no water at all
whyMenu.explain: Summer 2025's report describes partial credit as common here, with candidates omitting hydrated or omitting the oxidation state.

steps.working: The anhydrous calcium chloride is a drying agent: it removes the water (water vapour) from the air in the tube.
steps.decision: Say what it takes away, not what it keeps out. 'To prevent water getting in' is recorded as earning nothing, because the bung already does that.

steps.working: Tube C: the water was boiled first, which drives out the dissolved oxygen.
steps.decision: Start with why the oxygen has gone, then say what keeps it away. Two separate ideas, two marks.

steps.working: The oil layer then stops oxygen from dissolving back into the water, so the nail has no oxygen and cannot rust.
steps.decision: Use the word dissolving. 'To keep oxygen out' is not detailed enough for the mark.

workedExamples.finalAnswer: (a) Hydrated iron(III) oxide. (b) It is a drying agent: it removes water from the air in the tube. (c) The water was boiled to drive out the dissolved oxygen, and the layer of oil stops oxygen dissolving back in, so there is no oxygen and the nail cannot rust.

twin.stem: In the same experiment, explain why the nail in tube A, standing in ordinary tap water with air above it, does rust.

accepted: both water and oxygen are present, and rusting needs both

steps.working: Reactants Fe2O3 and CO; products Fe and CO2.
steps.decision: Write every formula before you balance. Carbon monoxide is CO and carbon dioxide is CO2 — one oxygen apart, and the difference is the whole reaction.

steps.working: Fe2O3 + 3CO → 2Fe + 3CO2. Two irons, so 2Fe; three oxygens to move, so 3CO and 3CO2.
steps.decision: Balance the iron first, then count the oxygens: 3 in the ore plus 3 in the carbon monoxide makes 6, and 3 carbon dioxides also hold 6.

steps.working: From the equation, one Fe2O3 gives two Fe, so 160 tonnes of the ore would give 2 × 56 = 112 tonnes of iron.
steps.decision: Take the ratio from the balanced equation, not from the formula. Missing the 2 in front of Fe halves the answer.
Write the line out before you use the calculator; a written substitution is what earns the method mark if the arithmetic slips.
Sense-check it: iron is most, but not all, of the ore, so the answer must be smaller than 320 and bigger than half of it.

twin.stem: Write the balanced symbol equation for the reaction that makes the reducing agent in the blast furnace, from carbon dioxide and coke.

items.stem: Which is higher in the reactivity series, zinc or iron?
items.skill: Prerequisite from §2.1 — you are not expected to have met rust prevention yet

options.feedback: Zinc is above iron, and that one fact is what makes galvanising and sacrificial protection work.
The order runs magnesium, aluminium, zinc, iron, copper, so zinc comes first. Section 4 of this lesson depends on it.
They sit at different heights, and the gap between them is what protects a galvanised bucket.

items.stem: What does reduction mean, in terms of oxygen?
items.skill: Prerequisite from the previous topic — oxidation and reduction with oxygen

options.feedback: Loss of oxygen. The whole blast furnace is one long example of it.
Gaining oxygen is oxidation. The redox topic sets this out, and section 6 here assumes it.
Reduction is not about mass; it is about losing oxygen, gaining hydrogen or gaining electrons.

items.stem: Which gas in the air makes up about a fifth of it and is needed for burning?
items.skill: Prerequisite from C2 §2.9 — the composition of air

options.feedback: Oxygen, about 21%. It is one of the two things rusting needs.
Nitrogen is the bigger share at about 78%, but it is very unreactive. The gas that matters here is oxygen.
Carbon dioxide is a very small part of the air and takes no part in rusting.

items.stem: What is the chemical name of rust?

options.feedback: Both marking words are there: hydrated, and the oxidation state of the iron.
That is half the answer. Rust has water built into it, so the name starts with hydrated — the word Summer 2025 examiners record as commonly omitted.
Also half. Iron forms two oxides, so the name has to say which: iron(III).
A hydroxide is a different compound. Rust is an oxide with water built into the solid, which is what hydrated means.

options.text: it removes the water from the air in the tube
options.feedback: It is a drying agent: it absorbs water that is already in the tube.

options.text: it stops water getting into the tube
options.feedback: The bung already does that. Examiners record this answer as earning nothing: the chemical removes water, it does not block it.

options.text: it removes the oxygen from the air
options.feedback: Removing oxygen is the other tube's job, done by boiling the water and adding oil.
That is the result, not the purpose. A general statement about preventing rust is not accepted.

items.stem: The water in one tube is boiled and then covered with a layer of oil. What is the oil for?
items.skill: State the purpose of the oil layer

options.text: it stops oxygen dissolving back into the water
options.feedback: The word dissolving is what earns it. Boiling removed the oxygen; the oil keeps it out of solution.
Examiners record this as too vague for the mark: say that it stops oxygen dissolving in the water.
The tube is stoppered, so evaporation is not the issue. The oil is there because of oxygen.

options.text: it kills bacteria in the water
options.feedback: Rusting is not biological. Examiners list sterilising as one of the wrong answers seen here.

options.text: magnesium is more reactive, so it corrodes instead of the iron
options.feedback: More reactive means it gives up its electrons first, so it is the one that goes.

options.text: the magnesium rusts in place of the iron
options.feedback: Only iron rusts; other metals corrode. Summer 2024 examiners recorded 'zinc rusting in place of iron' as not credited, and the same applies to magnesium.

options.text: magnesium is less reactive, so it protects the iron
options.feedback: It is the other way round. A less reactive metal, such as tin, makes a scratched object rust faster.

parts.stem:
Tube B holds an iron nail above a layer of anhydrous calcium chloride, and is stoppered.

parts.stem:
Tube C holds a nail in water that was boiled before the tube was set up, with a layer of oil floating on the water.
Explain the purpose of the layer of oil.

accepted: it stops oxygen dissolving back into the water

scheme.for: it prevents oxygen dissolving (redissolving) in the water
scheme.examinerNote: The word dissolving is what earns the mark; a general statement about keeping oxygen out is not credited.

hints: Boiling drove the dissolved oxygen out. What would happen without the oil?
parts.workedSolution: Boiling the water drove out the dissolved oxygen, and the oil layer stops oxygen from the air dissolving back into the water.

commonErrors.feedback: The idea is right but the mark needs one more word. Say that the oil stops oxygen dissolving in the water; 'keeps oxygen out' is recorded as not detailed enough.

parts.stem:
A steel bucket is galvanised.
Explain what galvanising is and how it protects the steel from rusting.

accepted: the steel is coated in zinc, and the zinc is more reactive than iron so it corrodes instead of the steel

scheme.for: the iron (steel) is coated in zinc
the zinc layer keeps water and oxygen off, and because zinc is more reactive than iron it corrodes in place of the iron even where the layer is scratched

hints: Name the metal first. The second mark is for how it protects.
Galvanising does two jobs at once, and either one earns the second mark.
parts.workedSolution: Galvanising is coating the iron or steel with zinc. The zinc acts as a barrier, keeping water and oxygen away, and because zinc is above iron in the reactivity series it also corrodes in place of the iron wherever the coating is scratched.

commonErrors.feedback: The important fact is missing: galvanising means coating the object in zinc. Summer 2025 examiners record candidates struggling with the term for exactly this reason.

context.setting: Magnesium blocks bolted to a buried steel pipeline

parts.stem:
Blocks of magnesium are bolted at intervals along a buried steel pipeline.
Explain how this stops the pipeline rusting. Use the reactivity series in your answer.

accepted: magnesium is more reactive than iron, so the magnesium corrodes instead of the iron

any: corrodes in place of the iron
reacts in place of the iron

scheme.for: magnesium is more reactive than iron (higher in the reactivity series)
so the magnesium corrodes (reacts) in place of the iron
scheme.examinerNote: Only iron rusts: another metal corrodes. Summer 2024 recorded 'zinc rusting in place of iron' as not credited.

hints: Compare the two metals first, then say what that makes the magnesium do.
Be careful with the verb: iron rusts, other metals corrode.
parts.workedSolution: Magnesium is above iron in the reactivity series, so it gives up its electrons more readily. It therefore corrodes in place of the iron, and the pipeline is left alone until the blocks are eaten away and replaced.

commonErrors.feedback: Only iron rusts; other metals corrode. Summer 2024 examiners recorded this exact wording as not credited. Say that the magnesium corrodes in place of the iron.

parts.stem:
A blast furnace is charged with 320 tonnes of iron(III) oxide. The equation is $\ce{Fe2O3 + 3CO -> 2Fe + 3CO2}$.
The relative formula mass of iron(III) oxide is 160 and the relative atomic mass of iron is 56.
Calculate the maximum mass of iron that could be obtained. Show your working. Give your answer to the nearest tonne.

scheme.for: the mass ratio from the equation: 160 of Fe2O3 gives 2 × 56 = 112 of Fe
substitution: 320 × 112 ÷ 160
224 (tonnes)

hints: Two iron atoms come out of every Fe2O3, so the top of the fraction is 112, not 56.
Sense-check: the answer must be less than the mass of ore you started with.
parts.workedSolution: One Fe2O3 gives two Fe, so 160 tonnes of ore would give 112 tonnes of iron. Scaling: 320 × 112 ÷ 160 = 224 tonnes.

The ratio is upside down: the answer came out bigger than the ore you started with, which cannot happen when only part of the ore is iron. Multiply by 112 and divide by 160.

parts.stem:
A boatyard wants to know why a steel hull rusts and how to stop it.
Describe an experiment that shows which conditions iron needs in order to rust, and explain two different ways of protecting the hull.
This question also assesses the quality of your written communication, including your use of specialist scientific terms.

bands.descriptor: Five or six of the indicative points, described in detail, with specialist chemical terms used widely and accurately; organised with clarity; spelling, punctuation and grammar good enough that the meaning is clear throughout.
Three or four of the indicative points; some specialist chemical vocabulary; organised with some clarity; spelling, punctuation and grammar competent enough for the meaning to be clear.
One or two of the indicative points; little specialist vocabulary; organisation may lack clarity; spelling, punctuation and grammar may leave the intended meaning unclear.

indicativeContent.point: set up identical stoppered tubes, each holding an iron nail, and leave them for the same time
one tube has water and air and acts as the control: its nail rusts
one tube has the water removed by a drying agent such as anhydrous calcium chloride, and its nail does not rust
one tube has boiled water under a layer of oil, so oxygen cannot dissolve in it, and its nail does not rust
the conclusion is that rusting needs both water and oxygen
a barrier method such as painting or galvanising keeps water and oxygen away from the steel
sacrificial protection bolts on a more reactive metal such as zinc or magnesium, which corrodes in place of the iron

scheme.for: banded: count the indicative points present, then place within the band on the quality of written communication — Band A [5]-[6] five or six points, Band B [3]-[4] three or four, Band C [1]-[2] one or two, [0] response not worthy of credit
scheme.examinerNote: A point contradicted elsewhere in the answer is not counted. Capital letters and full stops are part of the within-band judgement.

hints: An experiment needs a control as well as the tubes that change something.
Two protection methods that work in different ways score better than two barriers.
Name rust in full somewhere in the answer: it is one of the listed points.
parts.workedSolution: Set up three stoppered boiling tubes, each holding a clean iron nail, and leave them side by side for a week. The first holds the nail in ordinary tap water with air above it; this is the control, and its nail rusts, which shows what a normal result looks like. The second holds the nail in dry air above anhydrous calcium chloride, a drying agent that removes the water from the air; its nail does not rust. The third holds the nail in water that has been boiled to drive out the dissolved oxygen, with a layer of oil on top to stop oxygen dissolving back in; its nail does not rust either. Because a nail rusts only when both water and oxygen are present, rusting needs both, and the orange solid that forms is hydrated iron(III) oxide. The hull can be protected in two ways. A barrier method, such as painting it or galvanising it with a layer of zinc, keeps the water and the oxygen off the steel. Sacrificial protection bolts blocks of a more reactive metal, zinc or magnesium, onto the hull; because they are higher in the reactivity series they corrode in place of the iron, and they are replaced when they are eaten away.

findTheMistake.stem:
Aoife is asked: 'Give the chemical name of rust, and explain how galvanising protects steel. [4]'
Her answer:
studentWorking: Galvanising means the steel is coated in zinc.
The coating keeps water and oxygen away from the steel.
findTheMistake.whatWentWrong: Line 1 is missing both of its marking words. Rust is hydrated iron(III) oxide, and the scheme pays one mark for *hydrated* and one for the oxidation state, so 'iron oxide' collects neither. Lines 2 and 3 are both right: the metal is named, and the barrier is explained.
findTheMistake.feedback: Two of the four marks: galvanising is fully answered. What goes is the name, and it goes on two single words — *hydrated* and the *(III)*. Summer 2025 examiners recorded exactly those two as the ones candidates leave out, so they are worth rehearsing as words rather than as ideas.

prompts.prompt: Give the chemical name of rust, in full, and the two conditions iron needs to form it.
prompts.answer: Hydrated iron(III) oxide. Iron needs both water and oxygen.

prompts.prompt: In the rusting tubes experiment, what are the anhydrous calcium chloride and the layer of oil each for?
prompts.answer: The anhydrous calcium chloride is a drying agent that removes water from the air in the tube. The oil stops oxygen dissolving back into the boiled water.

prompts.prompt: Name four barrier methods of preventing rusting, and say what galvanising is.
prompts.answer: Painting, oiling or greasing, plastic coating, and galvanising. Galvanising is coating the iron with zinc.

prompts.prompt: Explain sacrificial protection in two steps, and say which verb goes with the protecting metal.
prompts.answer: A more reactive metal such as zinc or magnesium is attached to the iron, and because it gives up its electrons more readily it corrodes in place of the iron. The protecting metal corrodes; only iron rusts.

prompts.prompt: Name the three solids charged into a blast furnace and the gas blasted in at the base.
prompts.answer: Haematite, coke and limestone go in at the top; hot air is blasted in at the base.

prompts.prompt: Write the four blast-furnace equations in the order they happen.
prompts.answer: C + O2 → CO2; CO2 + C → 2CO; Fe2O3 + 3CO → 2Fe + 3CO2; CaCO3 → CaO + CO2, then CaO + SiO2 → CaSiO3.

prompts.prompt: Which of the two liquids at the base of the furnace is tapped off higher up, and why? And why is iron used for bridges?
prompts.answer: The slag, because it is less dense than the molten iron and floats on it. Iron is used in bridges and structures because of its strength.
